title: I. Kuzma Samsonov
paragraphs: But Dmitri knew nothing of what had happened to Grushenka. She had flown off to a new life and left him her last greetings, telling him to remember the hour of her love for ever. He was at that moment in a state of feverish agitation and activity. For the past two days his mind had been in such a wild condition that, as he said himself afterwards, he might easily have come down with brain fever. Alyosha had failed to find him the morning before, and Ivan had not managed to meet him at the tavern that same day. The people at his lodgings were hiding his movements, on his orders.

He had spent those two days literally rushing in every direction. He was “struggling with his destiny and trying to save himself,” as he put it afterwards. For some hours he even dashed out of town on urgent business, though it was terrible to him to lose sight of Grushenka for a moment. All this was explained in detail afterwards and confirmed by documents. For now, we will note only the most essential events of those two terrible days, just before the awful catastrophe that broke so suddenly over him.

It is true that Grushenka had loved him for an hour, genuinely and sincerely. Yet she sometimes tortured him cruelly and without mercy. The worst of it was that he could never tell what she meant to do. He could not win her over by force or by kindness. She would give way to nothing. She would only have grown angry and turned away from him altogether, and he knew that well already. He suspected, quite correctly, that she too was going through an inward struggle. She was in a state of extraordinary indecision, making up her mind to something and unable to settle on it. So, with good reason, he guessed with a sinking heart that at moments she must simply hate him and his passion. And perhaps she did. But what was troubling Grushenka he did not understand. For him, the whole tormenting question lay between himself and Fyodor Pavlovitch.

Here we must note, by the way, one certain fact. He was firmly convinced that Fyodor Pavlovitch would offer Grushenka lawful marriage, or perhaps had offered it already. He did not for a moment believe that the old lecher hoped to get what he wanted for three thousand roubles. Mitya had reached this conclusion from what he knew of Grushenka and her character. That was why he could believe at times that all Grushenka’s uneasiness came from not knowing which of them to choose, and which would be better for her.

Strange to say, during those days it never occurred to him to think about the “officer” coming back. This was the man who had had such a fatal influence on Grushenka’s life, and whose arrival she was expecting with such emotion and dread. It is true that lately Grushenka had been very quiet about it. Yet he knew perfectly well about a letter she had received a month ago from her seducer. He had heard of it from her own lips, and he partly knew what the letter said. In a moment of spite Grushenka had shown him that letter, but to her astonishment he attached hardly any importance to it. It would be hard to say why. Perhaps he was weighed down by the hideous horror of his struggle with his own father over this woman, and so could not imagine any more terrible danger, at least for the time being. He simply did not believe in a suitor who turned up suddenly after five years’ disappearance, and still less in his speedy arrival. Besides, the possibility of this new rival’s visit was only vaguely hinted at in the “officer’s” first letter, the one that was shown to Mitya. The letter was very indefinite, high-flown and full of sentimentality. It must be noted that Grushenka had hidden from him the last lines of the letter, where the man’s return was mentioned more definitely. He also remembered afterwards that at that moment he had noticed, on Grushenka’s face, a certain involuntary proud contempt for this message from Siberia. Grushenka told him nothing of what had passed later between her and this rival. So little by little he had completely forgotten the officer’s existence.

Whatever came later, and however things turned out, he felt that his final showdown with Fyodor Pavlovitch was near and had to be settled first. Every moment, with a sinking heart, he waited for Grushenka to decide. He always believed the decision would come suddenly, on a whim of the moment. Out of the blue she would say to him: “Take me, I’m yours for ever,” and that would be the end of it. He would seize her and sweep her off to the ends of the earth. Oh, then he would take her away at once, as far, far away as he could. To the farthest corner of Russia, if not of the earth. There he would marry her and settle down with her incognito, so that nobody would know anything about them, there, here, or anywhere. Then, oh, then, a new life would begin at once!

He dreamed feverishly at every moment of this different, reformed and “virtuous” life (“it must, it must be virtuous”). He thirsted for that reform and renewal. The filthy swamp where he had sunk of his own free will was too revolting to him. Like very many men in such cases, he put his faith above all in a change of place. If only it were not for these people, if only it were not for these circumstances, if only he could fly away from this accursed place—he would be completely regenerated and would start on a new path. That was what he believed in, and what he was yearning for.

But all of this depended on the first outcome, the _happy_ one. There was another possibility, a different and dreadful ending. Suddenly she might say to him: “Go away. I have just come to terms with Fyodor Pavlovitch. I am going to marry him and I don’t want you”—and then ... but then.... Mitya did not know what would happen then. He didn’t know it up to the last hour, and that must be said in his favor. He had no definite plans and had worked out no crime. He only watched and spied in agony, getting himself ready for the first, happy outcome of his fate. In fact, he pushed every other thought away. But even for that happy ending a quite different worry came up, a new and incidental difficulty, yet fatal and impossible to solve.

If she were to say to him: “I’m yours; take me away,” how could he take her away? Where did he have the means, the money to do it? It was just at this time that every source of income from Fyodor Pavlovitch dried up, the allowances that had gone on without a break for so many years. Grushenka had money, of course, but about this Mitya suddenly showed extraordinary pride. He wanted to carry her off and begin the new life with her himself, at his own expense, not hers. He could not imagine taking her money, and the very idea gave him a pang of intense revulsion. I won’t enlarge on this fact or analyze it here. I will only remark that this was his attitude at the moment. All this may have arisen indirectly and unconsciously from the secret stings of conscience over the money of Katerina Ivanovna, which he had dishonestly taken. “I’ve been a scoundrel to one of them, and I’ll soon be a scoundrel again to the other,” was what he felt then, as he explained afterwards, “and when Grushenka knows, she won’t care for such a scoundrel.”
So where was he to find the means? Where could he get this fateful money? Without it everything was lost and nothing could be done, “and all because I didn’t have the money. Oh, the shame of it!”

To get ahead of the story: he did, perhaps, know where to get the money, and perhaps he knew where it lay at that very moment. I will say no more about it here, since it will all become clear later. But his chief trouble, which I must explain however obscurely, was this. To have the sum he knew of, to _have the right_ to take it, he first had to pay back Katerina Ivanovna’s three thousand. If not, “I’m a common pickpocket, I’m a scoundrel, and I don’t want to begin a new life as a scoundrel,” Mitya decided. And so he made up his mind to move heaven and earth to return that three thousand to Katerina Ivanovna, and to do it _first of all_. He had reached the final stage of this decision, so to say, only in the last few hours. That was after his last meeting with Alyosha, two days before, on the high-road, on the evening when Grushenka had insulted Katerina Ivanovna. Mitya had heard Alyosha’s account of it and admitted that he was a scoundrel, and told Alyosha to tell Katerina Ivanovna so, if it could be any comfort to her. After parting from his brother that night, he had felt in his frenzy that it would be better “to murder and rob someone than fail to pay my debt to Katya. I’d rather everyone thought me a robber and a murderer, I’d rather go to Siberia than let Katya have the right to say that I deceived her and stole her money, and used her money to run away with Grushenka and begin a new life! That I can’t do!” So Mitya decided, grinding his teeth, and at times he might well imagine that his brain would give way. But meanwhile he went on struggling....

Oddly enough, you would have thought despair was all he had left. What chance did he have of raising such a sum, with nothing in the world? Yet right to the end he kept hoping he would get that three thousand, and that the money would somehow arrive of its own accord, as if it might fall from heaven. That is exactly how it is with people like Dmitri. The only dealings they have ever had with money have been squandering what came to them by inheritance, with no effort on their part, and they have no idea how money is earned. As soon as he parted from Alyosha two days earlier, a whirl of the most fantastic notions seized his brain and tangled his thoughts in confusion. That is why he fixed first on a perfectly wild undertaking. And perhaps for men of that kind in such circumstances, the most impossible and fantastic schemes are the first to occur to them, and look the most practical.

He suddenly decided to go to Samsonov, the merchant who was Grushenka’s protector, and propose a “scheme” to him. By means of it he would get from him at once the whole sum he needed. He had no doubt, not the slightest, of the commercial value of his scheme. He was only unsure how Samsonov would look on his freak, if he were to consider it from any but the commercial point of view. Mitya knew the merchant by sight, but he was not acquainted with him and had never spoken a word to him. For some unknown reason, though, he had long held the conviction that the old reprobate, who was lying at death’s door, would perhaps not object at all now to Grushenka’s securing a respectable position and marrying a man “to be depended upon.” And he believed not only that the old man would not object, but that this was what he wanted, and that he would be ready to help if the opportunity arose. From some rumor, or perhaps from some stray word of Grushenka’s, he had gathered besides that the old man would perhaps prefer him to Fyodor Pavlovitch for Grushenka.

Possibly many readers of my novel will feel that Dmitri showed great coarseness and lack of delicacy in reckoning on such help, and in being ready to take his bride, so to speak, from the hands of her protector. I will only observe that Mitya looked on Grushenka’s past as something completely over. He looked on that past with infinite pity. He resolved, with all the fervor of his passion, that once Grushenka told him she loved him and would marry him, it would mean the beginning of a new Grushenka and a new Dmitri, free from every vice. They would forgive one another and begin their lives afresh. As for Kuzma Samsonov, Dmitri saw him as a man who had had a fateful influence in that remote past of Grushenka’s, though she had never loved him. Now the old man was himself a thing of the past, completely done with and, so to say, non-existent. Besides, Mitya hardly looked on him as a man at all. It was known to everyone in the town that he was only a shattered wreck, and that his relations with Grushenka had changed their character and were now simply fatherly, and had been so for a long time.

Whatever one thinks of it, there was a great deal of simplicity in all this on Mitya’s part, for with all his vices he was a thoroughly simple-hearted man. Here is an example. Mitya seriously believed that old Kuzma, standing on the brink of the next world, must sincerely repent of his past relations with Grushenka. He believed that she had no more devoted friend and protector anywhere than this now harmless old man.

After his talk with Alyosha at the cross-roads he hardly slept all night. At ten o’clock the next morning he was at Samsonov’s house, telling the servant to announce him. It was a very large and gloomy old house of two stories, with a lodge and outhouses. On the lower floor lived Samsonov’s two married sons with their families, his old sister, and his unmarried daughter. In the lodge lived two of his clerks, one of whom also had a large family. Both the lodge and the lower floor were overcrowded, but the old man kept the upper floor to himself. He would not even let his daughter live there with him, though she waited on him. In spite of her asthma she had to run upstairs from below at certain fixed hours, and at any time he might call her.

The upper floor had a number of large rooms that were kept purely for show and furnished in the old-fashioned merchant style. Dull, long rows of clumsy mahogany chairs stood against the walls, glass chandeliers hung under covers, and gloomy mirrors hung on the walls. None of these rooms were ever used. The old man lived in one small, remote bedroom, where an old servant woman with a kerchief on her head looked after him, along with a lad who sat on the chest out in the passage. His legs were so swollen that he could barely walk. Only now and then was he lifted out of his leather armchair, and then the old woman held him up and walked him once or twice up and down the room. He was sullen and silent even with her.

When he was told that the “captain” had come, he refused flatly to see him. Mitya would not give up and sent up his name a second time. Samsonov questioned the lad closely. What did the man look like? Was he drunk? Would he make a scene? The answer was that he was sober, but he would not leave. The old man refused again. Mitya had expected this and had brought pencil and paper on purpose. He now wrote in a clear hand, “On most important business closely concerning Agrafena Alexandrovna,” and sent the note up.

Samsonov thought it over for a little. Then he told the lad to show the visitor into the drawing-room, and sent the old woman downstairs to tell his younger son to come up at once. This son was over six feet tall and uncommonly strong. He was clean-shaven and dressed in the European fashion, though his father still wore a kaftan and a beard. He came immediately and said nothing. The whole family trembled before the father. The old man had called for this giant, not because he was afraid of the “captain” (he was not at all a timid man), but to have a witness if anything went wrong. Leaning on his son and the servant lad, he waddled at last into the drawing-room. We may suppose he was very curious. The room where Mitya waited was vast and dreary, and it pressed down on the spirits. It had a double row of windows, a gallery, marbled walls, and three huge chandeliers hung with glass drops and covered with shades.

Mitya sat on a little chair near the entrance, waiting for his fate in nervous impatience. When the old man came in at the far door, seventy feet away, Mitya sprang up and went to meet him with his long, military stride. He was well dressed, in a buttoned-up frock-coat, with a round hat and black gloves in his hands. It was just how he had looked three days before at the elder’s, at the family meeting with his father and brothers. The old man stood waiting for him, dignified and unbending, and Mitya felt at once that the old man had looked him through and through as he came forward. He was also struck by Samsonov’s monstrously swollen face. The lower lip, always thick, now hung down like a bun. The old man bowed to his guest in dignified silence and waved him to a low chair by the sofa. Then, leaning on his son’s arm, he started to lower himself onto the sofa opposite, groaning with pain. Watching his struggle, Mitya at once felt remorse. He felt, too, how small he was in the presence of this dignified man he had dared to disturb.
“What do you want from me, sir?” said the old man, slowly, distinctly, sternly, but with courtesy, once he was finally seated.

Mitya jumped, leapt to his feet, then sat down again. Straight away he began to speak, loudly, in nervous haste, waving his arms, in a real frenzy. Anyone could see he was a man cornered, on the edge of ruin, clutching at his last straw and ready to go under if it failed him. Old Samsonov probably understood all this in an instant, though his face stayed as cold and still as a statue’s.

“Most honored sir, Kuzma Kuzmitch, you have surely heard more than once of my quarrels with my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, who robbed me of my inheritance from my mother ... seeing the whole town is gossiping about it ... for here everyone gossips about things they shouldn’t ... and besides, it might have reached you through Grushenka ... Sorry, through Agrafena Alexandrovna ... Agrafena Alexandrovna, the lady I hold in the highest respect and esteem ...”

So Mitya began, and he broke down at the very first sentence. We will not give his speech word for word, only the gist. Three months ago, he said, he had gone to a lawyer in the chief town of the province, “of express intention” (Mitya deliberately used these words in place of “intentionally”). “A distinguished lawyer, Kuzma Kuzmitch, Pavel Pavlovitch Korneplodov. Perhaps you’ve heard of him? A man of vast intellect, the mind of a statesman ... he knows you, too ... spoke of you in the highest terms ...” Mitya broke down again. But these breakdowns never stopped him. He took a leap across each gap and struggled on and on.

This Korneplodov had questioned him closely and looked over the documents he could bring (Mitya referred to these documents rather vaguely and hurried past the subject). He had then reported that they could certainly bring a suit over the village of Tchermashnya, which should have come to him, Mitya, from his mother, and so checkmate the old villain, his father ... “because not every door was shut, and justice might still find a loophole.” In short, he could count on another six or even seven thousand roubles from Fyodor Pavlovitch, because Tchermashnya was worth at least twenty-five thousand, he might say twenty-eight thousand, in fact “thirty, thirty, Kuzma Kuzmitch, and would you believe it, I didn’t get even seventeen out of that heartless man!” So he, Mitya, had dropped the matter for the moment, since he knew nothing about the law. But when he came here, a counter-claim against him left him dumbstruck (here Mitya lost his way again and again took a flying leap ahead). “So won’t you, excellent and honored Kuzma Kuzmitch, agree to take over all my claims against that unnatural monster, and pay me a lump sum of only three thousand?... You see, there’s no way you can lose by it. On my honor, my honor, I swear it. Quite the opposite, you could make six or seven thousand instead of three.” Above all he wanted it settled that very day.

“I’ll do the business with you at a notary’s, or wherever it’s done ... in fact, I’m ready to do anything.... I’ll hand over all the deeds ... whatever you want, I’ll sign anything ... and we could draw up the agreement right now ... and if it were possible, if it were only possible, this very morning.... You could pay me that three thousand, for there isn’t a capitalist in this town to compare with you, and so you would save me from ... save me, in fact ... for a good, I might say an honorable deed.... For I have the most honorable feelings for a certain person you know well, and look after like a father. I wouldn’t have come at all, if it weren’t as a father. And really, it’s a struggle of three in this business, for it’s fate—that’s a fearful thing, Kuzma Kuzmitch! A tragedy, Kuzma Kuzmitch, a tragedy! And since you dropped out long ago, it’s a tug-of-war between two. I’m putting it awkwardly, perhaps, but I’m not a literary man. You see, I’m on one side, and that monster on the other. So you must choose. It’s either me or the monster. It all lies in your hands—the fate of three lives, and the happiness of two.... Forgive me, I’m making a mess of it, but you understand ... I can see from your venerable eyes that you understand ... and if you don’t understand, I’m done for ... so you see!”

With that “so you see!” Mitya cut short his clumsy speech. He jumped up from his seat and waited for an answer to his foolish proposal. At that last phrase, he had suddenly realized, with despair, that it had all fallen flat, and above all that he had been talking utter nonsense.

“How strange! On the way here it seemed all right, and now it’s nothing but nonsense.” The thought dawned on his despairing mind all at once. The whole time he had been speaking, the old man had sat without moving, watching him with an icy look in his eyes. He kept Mitya in suspense for a moment. Then Kuzma Kuzmitch said, in the flattest and most chilling tone:
“Excuse me, we don’t take on such business.”
Mitya suddenly felt his legs going weak under him.
“What am I to do now, Kuzma Kuzmitch?” he muttered, with a pale smile. “It’s all up with me, I suppose—what do you think?”
“Excuse me....”
Mitya stayed on his feet, staring, unable to move. Then he noticed a stir in the old man’s face. He started.
“You see, sir, business of that kind isn’t in our line,” said the old man slowly. “There’s the court, and the lawyers—it’s pure misery. But if you like, there’s a man here you could go to.”
“Good heavens! Who is it? You’re my salvation, Kuzma Kuzmitch,” faltered Mitya.

“He doesn’t live here, and he isn’t here at the moment. He’s a peasant, and he deals in timber. His name is Lyagavy. For the past year he’s been haggling with Fyodor Pavlovitch over your copse at Tchermashnya. They can’t settle on a price, maybe you’ve heard? He’s back again now, and he’s staying with the priest at Ilyinskoe, about twelve versts from the Volovya station. He wrote to me about the copse as well, and asked my advice. Fyodor Pavlovitch means to go and see him himself. So if you got there before Fyodor Pavlovitch and made Lyagavy the offer you’ve made me, he might possibly—”

“A brilliant idea!” Mitya broke in, ecstatic. “He’s just the man, it would suit him perfectly. He’s haggling over it, they’re asking him too much, and here he’d be getting all the papers that give him title to the property itself. Ha ha ha!”
And Mitya suddenly let out his short, wooden laugh, which made Samsonov start.
“How can I thank you, Kuzma Kuzmitch?” cried Mitya, gushing.
“Don’t mention it,” said Samsonov, with a nod of his head.
“But you don’t know, you’ve saved me. Oh, it was a true presentiment that brought me to you.... So now, off to this priest!”
“There’s no need to thank me.”
“I’ll make haste and fly there. I’m afraid I’ve worn out your strength. I’ll never forget this. A Russian is telling you that, Kuzma Kuzmitch, a R-r-russian!”
“Of course!”
Mitya reached out and seized his hand to shake it, but a spiteful gleam showed in the old man’s eye. Mitya drew back his hand, then at once scolded himself for his distrust.
“It’s because he’s tired,” he thought.

“For her sake! For her sake, Kuzma Kuzmitch! You understand that it’s for her,” he cried, and his voice rang through the room. He bowed, spun around, and with the same long stride went to the door without looking back. He was trembling with joy.

“Everything was on the edge of ruin, and my guardian angel has saved me,” he thought. If a businessman like Samsonov (a most worthy old man, and what dignity!) had suggested this way out, then ... then success was certain. He would fly off at once. “I’ll be back before night, I’ll be back tonight and it will be done. Could the old man have been laughing at me?” cried Mitya, as he strode toward his lodging. He could think of nothing else, of course, except that this was practical advice, “from such a businessman,” who knew the business and who knew this Lyagavy (curious name!). Or else the old man was laughing at him.

Alas! It was the second. Long afterward, when the catastrophe had happened, old Samsonov himself admitted, with a laugh, that he had made a fool of the “captain.” He was a cold, spiteful, sarcastic man, with a streak of violent dislikes. Maybe it was the “captain’s” excited face. Maybe it was the foolish certainty of this “rake and spendthrift” that Samsonov could be taken in by a cock-and-bull story like his scheme. Maybe it was jealousy over Grushenka, in whose name the “scapegrace” had burst in on him with such a tale, to get money. Something worked on the old man, but I can’t say what. But at the moment when Mitya stood before him, feeling his legs go weak and crying wildly that he was ruined, the old man looked at him with intense spite and made up his mind to turn him into a laughing-stock. When Mitya had gone, Kuzma Kuzmitch, white with rage, turned to his son and ordered him to see that the beggar was never seen again, and never let into the yard, or else he’d—

He did not say what he would do. But even his son, who often saw him in a rage, shook with fear. For a whole hour afterward the old man trembled with anger, and by evening he was worse and sent for the doctor.
